alt: Two graphs of population size over time. The J-curve rises exponentially with no limit and then crashes when resources run out. The S-curve has lag, exponential and transitional phases, then a plateau at the carrying capacity K held by negative feedback.
caption: Limiting factors turn exponential growth into a plateau at carrying capacity.

alt: Three steps: 40 beetles are caught and marked, then released to mix back into the population; a week later 50 are caught, of which 8 are marked. The Lincoln index gives N = 40 × 50 ÷ 8 = 250 beetles.
caption: The share of marked animals in the second catch scales up to the whole population.

alt: Two flow diagrams with widths proportional to energy. Producers: GPP of 18 500 kJ per square metre per year splits into 11 100 lost as heat in respiration and NPP of 7400. Grasshoppers: 1850 eaten, 1110 lost in faeces, leaving GSP of 740; 592 is respired, leaving NSP of 148.
caption: Subtract respiration for NPP and NSP; for consumers, subtract faeces first.

alt: Four trophic levels stacked: producers 10 000 units, primary consumers 1000, secondary 100 and tertiary 10, with about 10% passing up each step and the rest lost as heat. A side panel lists the reasons for loss and a worked example: 666 ÷ 7400 × 100 = 9.0%.
caption: About 10% passes to the next level; the rest leaves as heat, so chains are short.

alt: Three pyramids. Numbers can be inverted: one oak supports thousands of caterpillars. Biomass can be inverted in water: phytoplankton support a larger standing mass of zooplankton. Productivity is never inverted because each level receives only a fraction of the energy below.
caption: Only the pyramid of productivity can never be inverted.

alt: Systems diagram of the carbon cycle. Storages: atmosphere, producers, consumers, oceans, soil organic matter, fossil fuels and limestone. Flows: photosynthesis, respiration, feeding, death and waste, decomposition, dissolving and release at the ocean surface, sedimentation and fossilisation, and combustion, which humans have greatly speeded up.
caption: Name the storage and the flow: humans mainly speed up combustion and remove sinks.

alt: Cycle diagram. Nitrogen gas is fixed to ammonium by bacteria, Rhizobium and the Haber process; nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrite then nitrate, which plants assimilate. Animals feed on plants, dead matter and waste are ammonified back to ammonium, denitrifying bacteria return nitrate to N₂ in waterlogged soil, and nitrate can leach into water.
caption: Nitrification needs oxygen; denitrification happens in anaerobic, waterlogged soil.
